We’re rolling out changes to make Fable 5’s safeguards for frontier LLM development visible.

Starting this week, flagged requests will visibly fall back to Opus 4.8—the same as our safeguards for cyber and bio. You will see this every time it happens. On the API, any flagged requests will return a reason for their refusal (coming to server-side fallback in the next few days).

We wanted to deploy Fable 5 to our users quickly and safely. Visible safeguards can be probed, so they have to be robust, which takes time to get right. Invisible safeguards can be targeted more narrowly, allowing us to ship quickly with very few false positives. We went with invisible safeguards for this reason—and that was the wrong tradeoff. You should have visibility into the safeguards we have in place, and why. We’re sorry for not getting the balance right.

Making the safeguards visible makes them easier to work around, so keeping them robust to jailbreaks will unfortunately mean more false positives while we improve the classifiers. We're also tuning our bio and cyber classifiers to trigger less often on harmless requests. We know this is frustrating and we’ll do our best to keep this period as short as possible.

If you think a request has been mistakenly flagged: run /feedback in Claude Code, click thumbs-down on the fallback in https://t.co/LtktniD5HY or Cowork, or file the safeguard appeal form for API requests. Your reports help us tune these classifiers and we appreciate your feedback.   
https://t.co/TDAAYRGqDt

Claude Fable 5’s "ranking factors" leaked.

Buried inside thousands of lines is one of the clearest explanations we have seen of how Claude decides which websites to search, open, cite and potentially recommend.

It also explains why some businesses repeatedly appear in Claude while others remain invisible.

Let’s go through it.

And if you want to see whether Claude, ChatGPT, Google AI, Perplexity and Grok are recommending your business right now, start here (it's free):

https://t.co/Pn764BHwyL

One important caveat before we get into the details.

Anthropic did not publish this as an official Claude ranking guide.

The prompt was extracted and published by a public system-prompt archive, so I would not treat every sentence as a permanent ranking factor.

But the search instructions are specific enough to reveal the process Claude is being told to follow.

And that process has major implications for SEO and AI search optimization.

The first major revelation is fairly straightforward.

When Claude searches the web, its search tool returns 10 highly ranked results.

That is the initial pool Claude is working from for that individual search.

The prompt does not say those are specifically Google’s top 10 results.

It says Claude receives 10 highly ranked results from a search engine, and Claude can run multiple searches using different queries.

So ranking in Google’s top 10 does not automatically guarantee that Claude will consider your business.

What the prompt does confirm is that ranked search visibility plays a major role in determining which websites Claude encounters first.

Claude starts with a small group of pages that a search engine has already ranked highly.

This means traditional search visibility still matters.

A lot.

If your page never enters those initial groups of ranked results, Claude may never open it, evaluate it or cite it for that particular question.

Ranking creates the opportunity to be considered.

And this is the starting point for all SEO Stuff (https://t.co/wKpf0EILTx) customers, big and small. 

Claude then applies another layer of evaluation.

This is where things get more interesting.

The prompt tells Claude to begin with very short, broad searches, generally between one and six words, before narrowing the query when necessary.

That means Claude may search phrases like:

Best payroll software

Dental marketing agency

Business insurance companies

CRM for contractors

Claude may reduce the user’s longer question into several shorter searches and investigate the category from different directions.

The next part is my interpretation of what those instructions mean for businesses, rather than language Anthropic explicitly included in the prompt.

This is why semantic alignment matters.

Your website needs to make it extremely obvious:

What your company does

Which category it belongs to

Who it serves

Which problems it solves

Which products or services it should be compared against

If Claude searches five different versions of your category and your site is not clearly aligned with any of them, you are unlikely to enter the candidate pool.

One generic homepage is rarely enough to cover all of those searches.

You need pages that clearly map the different ways buyers describe the category, problem, use case and desired outcome.

Claude’s prompt then says that it must search when a question involves:

Current information

Recently released products

Specific models or versions

Companies whose status may have changed

Unfamiliar entities

Comparisons and rankings involving newer options

This is a huge point.

Claude is explicitly instructed to use the live web when its existing knowledge may be outdated.

That means brands cannot depend entirely on what Claude may have learned about them months or years ago.

You need current pages.

Current comparisons.

Current product information.

Current pricing.

Current case studies.

Current reviews.

Current third-party mentions.

There is some nuance here.

The prompt does not say that newer pages automatically outrank older pages across every topic.

Claude is told to prioritize recent sources when the subject changes quickly or when the answer may have changed.

Freshness is especially important for things like prices, products, company information, regulations, rankings and current recommendations.

For more stable subjects, an older authoritative source may still be completely appropriate.

Claude Fable 5 has a reliable knowledge cutoff in early 2026. 

Anything that happened after that may require live retrieval.

And that retrieval creates a new opportunity for businesses that were previously too small, too new or too unknown to appear in Claude’s stored knowledge.

Your company may not be deeply represented in the model’s existing knowledge.

But it can still become one of the sources Claude finds today.

This is where SEO Stuff’s done-for-you package becomes especially relevant:

https://t.co/yEFyM0Ze7W

This combines 10 AI search optimized pieces of content with three DR50+ contextual PR backlinks.

The content creates the category, use-case and comparison pages Claude can discover through different searches.

The backlinks help those pages compete inside the ranked search layer Claude uses to build its initial source pool.

To be clear, Claude’s prompt does not explicitly name backlinks, Domain Rating or DR50+ placements as direct Claude ranking factors.

That is my interpretation of how businesses can improve their chances of appearing in the ranked search results Claude uses for discovery.

Claude’s prompt also says search snippets are often insufficient.

After finding a potentially useful result, Claude is instructed to open the page and retrieve the complete content.

Getting into the search results is only the first step.

The page itself still has to deliver.

Claude needs to determine:

What the page is about

Which question it answers

What factual claims it supports

Which passages are relevant

Whether the information is current

Whether the source is credible

The prompt does not explicitly prescribe question-based headings, comparison tables, schema or short answer blocks as direct ranking factors.

The next recommendations are my interpretation of how to make a page easier for Claude to evaluate, extract from and cite once it has been opened.

This is why clear structure matters.

Question-based headings.

Direct answer blocks.

Specific definitions.

Comparison tables.

Dates.

Named products.

Clear authorship.

Original research.

Transparent sourcing.

Pages filled with vague marketing language give Claude very little usable material.

Pages organized around specific questions and factual answers give it reusable evidence.

Claude’s system prompt then reveals something even more important.

It tells Claude to favor original sources.

Examples include:

Company websites

Official documentation

Government sources

Peer-reviewed research

Primary reports

This means your own website can absolutely become the source Claude cites.

Your website needs to contain original information worth citing.

That could include:

Your actual pricing

Original research

Industry data

Product specifications

Customer results

Methodology

Company policies

Detailed case studies

Expert explanations

Clear documentation

A generic article that repeats the same information already available across dozens of competing sites gives Claude very little reason to select your page as the source.

The Premium Content Bundle is built around solving this at scale:

https://t.co/4CAnUt07PO

It creates 60 long-form pieces of content mapped across the questions, comparisons and use cases surrounding your category.

Each article covers a different part of the category instead of repeating the same generic topic.

The broader objective is to build enough specific category coverage that Claude keeps encountering your business while researching different parts of the buyer’s question.

Claude also uses more searches for open-ended recommendation questions.

A simple factual question may require one search.

A broad recommendation or comparison can trigger several searches across multiple products, categories and sources.

That means category coverage compounds.

One ranking page gives you one opportunity.

A connected group of highly relevant pages gives you many opportunities to enter Claude’s research process.

But there is another side to this.

The prompt explicitly warns Claude to be more skeptical when reviewing search results for product recommendations.

Why?

Because those results are heavily influenced by SEO and may be inaccurate or misleading.

That is probably the most important part of the entire leak for businesses.

Claude uses ranked search results as a discovery layer while applying additional scrutiny to commercial claims.

A page claiming that your company is the best option is not enough on its own.

My interpretation is that Claude will be more confident when that claim is supported by:

Independent reviews

Authoritative third-party mentions

Customer evidence

Relevant certifications

Original data

Transparent comparisons

Consistent information across multiple sources

This creates a two-layer system in which your own website provides the first-party facts and trusted external websites provide additional validation.

That is why authority-building still matters even when Claude favors original sources.

Your website tells Claude what the business offers, who it serves and why it is different.

Trusted external websites help establish that those claims are credible.

This is where SEO Stuff’s Premium Authority Bundle fits:

https://t.co/Z9m9D7TjES

It places three contextual PR backlinks on DR50+ domains that already have real search authority.

Again, the prompt does not say Claude directly measures Domain Rating or treats backlinks as an explicit recommendation factor.

The practical interpretation is that those placements can help a business compete in the ranked search systems Claude uses while also creating third-party evidence that supports the brand’s claims.

The prompt also reveals that Claude must cite specific claims drawn from web searches.

This changes how content should be written.

Claude needs passages capable of supporting individual statements, rather than pages that are only broadly related to the topic.

For example:

When was the product launched?

How much does it cost?

Who is it designed for?

What feature makes it different?

What measurable result did a customer achieve?

What evidence supports the company’s claim?

The more clearly your page answers those questions, the easier it becomes for Claude to use it as evidence.

“Claim-sized content blocks” is my term, not language used in the system prompt.

But it is a useful way to think about the type of content Claude can retrieve and cite.

One clear question.

One direct answer.

One supporting fact.

One source or piece of evidence.

That is far more useful to Claude than 1,500 words of general brand copy.

The system prompt also says Claude products do not allow advertisers to pay for conversational promotion.

There is no sponsored shortcut into Claude’s answers.

Businesses have to earn their way into the source pool through visibility, relevance, freshness and credibility.

There is one more layer worth discussing.

Claude can personalize recommendations using information it remembers about the user, including their preferences and interests.

That means the company Claude recommends can change depending on:

Industry

Company size

Location

Budget

Use case

Technical requirements

Previous preferences

This is why businesses need more than a page targeting “best software” or “best agency.”

You need to clearly explain who the offering is best for.

Best accounting software for agencies.

Best insurance provider for multi-location businesses.

Best CRM for home service companies.

The more clearly your pages map the offering to a specific buyer, the easier it becomes for Claude to justify recommending it to that person.

If I had to reduce this entire prompt to one core idea, it would be this:

Claude uses ranked search results to discover candidates.

It opens pages to find usable evidence.

It favors current and original sources when appropriate.

It cites specific factual claims.

It applies additional skepticism to commercial recommendations.

It looks for corroboration before trusting marketing claims.

And it can personalize the final recommendation around the person asking.

To show up consistently, my interpretation is that your business needs to be:

Ranked highly enough to be discovered

Clearly positioned enough to match the query

Structured well enough to be extracted

Current enough for time-sensitive questions

Specific enough to be cited

Validated enough to be recommended

This is the system SEO Stuff was built around:

https://t.co/eh1auroJF7

And if you want to see whether your business is already being recommended across Claude, ChatGPT, Google AI, Perplexity and Grok, check here:

https://t.co/Pn764BHwyL

62% of Google's AI Overview citations are going to pages outside the top 10 search results.

That means the majority of AI-driven recommendations in your category are going to other brands.

If you want to capture a share of that 62%, here is how:

According to Ahrefs's February 2026 study of 863,000 SERPs and 4 million AI Overview URLs, only 38% of AI Overview citations now come from pages ranking in the top 10.

A year ago that number was 76%.

[If you want to see what ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and broader AI search is saying about your business right now, start here (it's free):  

https://t.co/Pn764BHwyL]

According to the same data, 31% of citations now come from pages ranking beyond position 100 for the original search query.

Your page-one rankings still matter, but they are only getting you into 38% of the AI citation opportunities in your category. The other 62% is going to whoever covered the questions you did not.

And that is what SEO Stuff (https://t.co/wKpf0EILTx) helps businesses capture.

Here is what changed: Google upgraded to Gemini 3 as the default for AI Overviews. That upgrade expanded how aggressively AI Overviews break buyer queries into sub-searches. 

When a buyer searches "best CRM for small business," Google's AI no longer just looks at pages ranking for that exact phrase. It internally generates sub-queries like "CRM onboarding time comparison 2026" and "CRM pricing for teams under 10," then pulls sources from those results too.

Again, if you want to see where your brand is being cited in AI Overviews and where competitors are capturing citations instead, start here (it's free):

https://t.co/Pn764BHwyL

Your page ranks position 3 for your primary keyword. That still gets you cited in the 38% of AI Overviews that pull from the top 10. But a competitor who has pages ranking for those sub-queries is eligible for the other 62%. 

And according to Ahrefs, 31% of all AI Overview citations are coming from pages that rank beyond position 100 for the original search. These are pages that would never appear in traditional Google results. But they answer a specific sub-question the AI generated internally, and that was enough to get cited and recommended to the buyer.

The brands capturing that 62% share two things.

The first is content depth. Not 5 or 10 pages targeting primary keywords, but 40 to 60 pages covering every question a buyer in your category actually asks: comparison queries, specification queries, use-case queries, integration queries, pricing breakdowns. Every page you have that answers one of those sub-questions is another chance to get cited. Every sub-question you have not covered is a citation going to a competitor instead.

The second is authority. You can have 60 pages covering every sub-question, but if your domain does not carry enough authority to rank for those sub-queries, the pages sit uncited. According to Ahrefs, the citation system still requires ranking well enough to appear in the AI's retrieval set. The difference is that now you need to rank across a much wider set of queries. That requires domain-level authority from editorial backlinks that lifts everything, not just a few links pointed at your homepage.

Remember, if you want to see where your brand stands across Google AI Overviews and where the gaps are, start here (it's free):

https://t.co/Pn764BHwyL

Here is what all this looks like in practice:

A buyer searches "best project management tool for agencies." Google's AI breaks that into sub-queries and pulls sources for each one. Brand A has 60 pages of expert-written content covering every sub-question in the project management category, backed by editorial backlinks from trusted publications. Brand B has a homepage and 5 feature pages targeting primary keywords.

Brand A gets cited in the AI Overview. Brand B does not. The buyer reads the AI answer, sees Brand A recommended, and clicks through. Brand B's page-one ranking for the primary keyword did not help because the AI pulled most of its sources from sub-queries where Brand B had no content.

The opportunity here is straightforward. Your page-one rankings are still working for 38% of AI citations. The other 62% is available to any brand willing to build the content depth and authority to capture it. The brands doing this now are locking in citation positions that will be harder to displace as competition increases.

Here is what to do with this:

Map the sub-questions buyers ask in your category beyond your primary keywords. Comparison queries, specification queries, use-case queries, integration queries. If you do not have pages covering those, you are leaving 62% of AI citations to competitors.

Build domain-level authority that lifts your ranking strength across the full query set. Backlinks from trusted editorial domains raise your entire domain, making every page more likely to appear in the AI's retrieval set for sub-queries.

Think category coverage, not keyword coverage. The brands capturing the 62% are the ones whose content answers every question in the category. The brands missing it are the ones who stopped at their top 10 keywords.

This is the system SEO Stuff (https://t.co/wKpf0EILTx) was built around.

Expert-attributed content backed by DR50+ backlinks: the content covers the sub-questions AI Overviews are actually searching when buyers ask about your category, and the backlinks give your domain the authority to rank for them

The content package:

https://t.co/4CAnUt07PO

60 pages of expert-attributed content covering the sub-questions in your category that AI Overviews pull from when assembling answers across every major query in your space

The authority package:

https://t.co/Z9m9D7TjES

Domain-level authority from trusted editorial sites that lifts your ranking strength across the wider query set AI Overviews now draw from

Your page-one rankings are capturing 38% of AI citations in your category. The other 62% is going to whoever built the content depth and authority to cover the sub-questions. That is the opportunity, and the brands building now are the ones who will own it.

6 months ago I one-shotted a game where you're walking down the street and the goal is to wave to good guys and flip off bad guys

I used Gemini 3 Pro, ThreeJS and MediaPipe

Today I used Claude Fable 5 and a similar prompt and it cooked this game in minutes
 
@threejs @claudeai https://t.co/Pqdqa4ltBg

Claude Fable 5 is a beast at creating full landing pages with a complete on-scroll experience from just one prompt 😱 

Since this new model just came out and is more expensive, I didn’t want to waste credits testing random prompts, so I planned everything carefully before using it.

On-scroll experience has always been one of my weaknesses, and I’ve been trying to understand how to make it better. I think I finally found a workflow that works for me.

I picked a website for inspiration, recorded the full landing page while scrolling, and used Codex to analyze the website and the video. It created screenshots, broke down the on-scroll experience, and helped me write a very detailed prompt to recreate the same type of motion, but with a completely different brand, color palette, text, and visual direction.

Then I gave that prompt to Claude Fable 5, attached the full landing page screenshots, and asked it to build the whole landing page in one shot.

The result is honestly crazy. It created pinned scroll sections, oversized typography, floating 3D cards, expanding gallery grids, product mockups, a profile builder, a community board, and even an on-load animation.

I’m currently recording this full workflow to teach you how I planned the prompt, analyzed the reference website, broke down the on-scroll experience, and used Claude Fable 5 to build the landing page in one shot.

https://t.co/EeOEy9VViy 的架构.

第一件: Anthropic 发布 Fable 5, 第 5 代模型, 定位直接是 hardest knowledge work and hardest coding problems. 不是辅助工具, 是任务的原生执行者. 定价 $10/M input + $50/M output, prompt cache 打到九折.

第二件: Postman 的 Ruben Casas 在 AI Engineer 大会讲 Generative UI for MCP Apps. 他把 UI 生成分成三档.

Static 调预定义组件, 快但僵硬
Declarative LLM 生成 JSON/YAML, runtime 映射到组件, 他认为是今天最务实的平衡点
Generative LLM 当场直接写 HTML/CSS/JS, 没有组件这一层

他演示了一个 weather agent. 单次工具调用, 直接生成带搜索框 + blur 动画 + 默认开 accessibility 的天气查询界面. 没有 React 组件, 没有 prebuilt template.

关键约束是 containment, LLM 生成的代码必须跑在 sandbox 里. MCP apps 把 double iframe 设为默认架构, 不是 over-engineering, 是 generative UI 能进 production 的前提.

他最后用了一个类比: 第一批电视节目就是带摄像头拍摄的广播, 因为那时没人能想象电视该长什么样. 我们现在做 agent UI, 就是 1950 年那个时刻.

这两件事让我直接回头审了自己的产品.

https://t.co/EeOEy9VViy Playground 早期, 我用 React 组件库画 finding 卡片. 每个 finding 一个 card, severity 用 color badge, category 用 icon, 看起来标准化. 但一直觉得不对, 同样是 high severity, credential exposure 和 prompt injection 应该被不同表达, 组件库统一规格反而把 nuance 抹平了.

后来改成 LLM 直接 render finding 卡片, 给它一个 sandbox 约束: 不能执行 shell, 不能访问 /etc, 输出必须是 markdown. 其他的让 LLM 根据 finding 的具体 nature 自己决定怎么展示.

改完之后 https://t.co/EeOEy9VViy 才第一次长得像 AI 原生产品, 不像套了 AI 壳的传统 SaaS.

这两件事合起来说的是同一件事: 组件正在消解为生成 + 沙箱两件事.

模型负责生成, 系统负责设边界. 这才是 AI 时代真正的 composability, 不是把零件拼起来, 是给模型设好能玩耍的笼子.

Fable 5 这种 5 代模型上线之后, 我会反复问自己: 我现在做的这一层, 是在拼组件, 还是在设边界? 拼组件的那层很可能 6 个月内被生成 + 沙箱替代.

React 组件库不是 AI 时代的资产, sandbox 设计才是.

Two unrelated things happened this week that turned out to be the same thing at different layers.

Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5 on June 9. Fifth-generation model. Positioned directly at "the hardest knowledge work and coding problems." $10/M input, $50/M output, 90% prompt cache discount. The Every team ran a week of testing. The signal in the positioning isn't subtle: the model itself is now the native executor of the task. Not a component in a pipeline. The whole pipeline.

Then I watched Ruben Casas from Postman speak at AI Engineer on generative UI for MCP apps. His core question: frontier models already write better frontend code than most engineers do by hand, so why is almost every agent UI still calling prebuilt React component libraries?

He laid out three tiers.

Static — call predefined components. Fast, rigid. AG UI and Goose's auto visualizer live here.
Declarative — LLM generates JSON or YAML, a runtime engine maps to components. He called this the most pragmatic balance point today.
Generative — LLM writes HTML, CSS, JavaScript directly. No component layer at all. His weather agent demo: one tool call, a search box, blur animations, accessibility on by default. No React. No template. Generated from context.

The critical constraint for generative UI is containment. LLM-generated code must run inside a sandbox. That's exactly why MCP apps default to a double iframe architecture. It's not over-engineering. It's the prerequisite for shipping generative UI to production.

His closing analogy: the first TV programs were just radio shows with a camera pointed at them, because nobody could yet imagine what television should look like. Agent UI in June 2026 is that moment.

Three layers are moving in the same direction simultaneously.

Model layer: Fable 5 takes the whole task directly. No manual decomposition into small chunks to feed the model piece by piece.

UI layer: Generative UI stops asking which React component the model should call. The system's job becomes sandbox + constraints, not maintaining a component library.

Workflow layer where I live every day: I built the early https://t.co/2oU9IRNgBi Playground with a React component library for rendering finding cards. Each finding got a card, severity got a color badge, category got an icon. Looked clean. But credential exposure and prompt injection both graded High Severity, and they read identically — the component spec flattened the nuance. The standardization was actually erasing information.

Switched to letting LLM render the cards directly with a sandbox constraint: SKILL.md can't execute shell, can't access /etc, output must be markdown. Everything else belongs to the model. After that change, https://t.co/2oU9IRNgBi finally looked like an AI-native product instead of a SaaS with an AI wrapper.

Components are dissolving into two things: generation and sandbox. Model handles generation. System sets the boundary. That's what composability actually means in the AI era. Not assembling parts. Building the right cage for the model to play in.

If you're building something right now, map each layer. Which parts are still assembling components, which parts are already generation + sandbox. The component-assembly layers aren't assets. The sandbox design is.
